claim: From March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022, there were 1,065,200 (95% CI 909,800–1,218,000) excess all-cause deaths in the United States.
source: Over the study period, we estimate an excess of 1,065,200 (95% Confidence Interval (CI) 909,800–1,218,000) all-cause deaths, of which 80% are reflected in official COVID-19 statistics.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the study's excess mortality analysis using time series approaches applied to US mortality data.

claim: 80% of excess all-cause deaths from March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022 are reflected in official COVID-19 statistics.
source: Over the study period, we estimate an excess of 1,065,200 (95% Confidence Interval (CI) 909,800–1,218,000) all-cause deaths, of which 80% are reflected in official COVID-19 statistics.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison between estimated excess deaths and official COVID-19 death statistics.

claim: State-specific excess death estimates are highly correlated with SARS-CoV-2 serology.
source: State-specific excess death estimates are highly correlated with SARS-CoV-2 serology, lending support to our approach.
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between excess mortality estimates and CDC seroprevalence surveys.

claim: Mortality from 7 of the 8 studied conditions rose during the pandemic, with the exception of cancer.
source: Mortality from 7 of the 8 studied conditions rose during the pandemic, with the exception of cancer.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of cause-specific mortality data during the pandemic period.

claim: 84% (95% CI 65–94%) of all-cause excess mortality can be statistically attributed to the direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: We find that 84% (95% CI 65–94%) of all-cause excess mortality can be statistically attributed to the direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
evidence: The claim is based on generalized additive models (GAM) fitted to excess mortality data using covariates for direct and indirect pandemic effects.

claim: At least 67% of mortality from diabetes, Alzheimer's, heart diseases, and all-cause mortality among individuals over 65 years can be attributed to the direct contribution of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: We also estimate a large direct contribution of SARS-CoV-2 infection (≥67%) on mortality from diabetes, Alzheimer's, heart diseases, and in all-cause mortality among individuals over 65 years.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis of cause-specific and age-specific mortality data.

claim: Indirect effects predominate in mortality from external causes and all-cause mortality among individuals under 44 years.
source: In contrast, indirect effects predominate in mortality from external causes and all-cause mortality among individuals under 44 years, with periods of stricter interventions associated with greater rises in mortality.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis showing stronger associations with intervention stringency than with COVID-19 intensity.

claim: Periods of stricter interventions are associated with greater rises in mortality among individuals under 44 years.
source: In contrast, indirect effects predominate in mortality from external causes and all-cause mortality among individuals under 44 years, with periods of stricter interventions associated with greater rises in mortality.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis using the Oxford stringency index as a covariate.

claim: By the end of January 2023, official statistics reported 1,056,000 COVID-19 deaths in the United States.
source: By the end of January 2023, official statistics reported 1,056,000 deaths in the United States alone (Johns Hopkins University, 2022), although burden estimates that do not rely on official tallies suggest a higher death toll (Weinberger et al., 2020; Karlinsky and Kobak, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to Johns Hopkins University data.

claim: Burden estimates that do not rely on official tallies suggest a higher COVID-19 death toll than official statistics.
source: By the end of January 2023, official statistics reported 1,056,000 deaths in the United States alone (Johns Hopkins University, 2022), although burden estimates that do not rely on official tallies suggest a higher death toll (Weinberger et al., 2020; Karlinsky and Kobak, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on excess mortality.

claim: Non-COVID-19 deaths increased in Spring of 2020 at the height of the first wave in part due to avoidance of the healthcare system.
source: A pandemic of the magnitude of COVID-19 would be expected to have secondary effects on unrelated health conditions; for instance, non-COVID-19 deaths increased in Spring of 2020 at the height of the first wave in part due to avoidance of the healthcare system (Bollmann et al., 2020; Kansagra et al., 2020; Mafham et al., 2020; Woolf et al., 2020; Woolf et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Excess mortality approaches have been used for over a century to capture the full scope of large-scale infectious disease events, heatwaves, and earthquakes.
source: Excess mortality approaches have been used for over a century to capture the full scope of large-scale infectious disease events, heatwaves, and earthquakes, by measuring the rise in mortality over a historical baseline (Serfling, 1963; Weinberger et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to historical and recent literature on excess mortality methods.

claim: In the early phase of the pandemic, excess mortality approaches highlighted substantial underestimation in official statistics of COVID-19 deaths due to limited viral testing.
source: In the early phase of the pandemic, these approaches highlighted substantial underestimation in official statistics of COVID-19 deaths due to limited viral testing (Weinberger et al., 2020; Kobak, 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on excess mortality during the pandemic.

claim: Deaths triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection could result from a complicated and protracted pathologic process, especially in patients with multiple underlying chronic conditions.
source: Additionally, a number of deaths triggered by SARS-CoV-2 infection could result from a complicated and protracted pathologic process, especially in patients with multiple underlying chronic conditions, who may lack a history of SARS-CoV-2 testing, and whose death may not be ascribed to COVID-19.
evidence: The claim is based on logical inference about disease pathology and death certification processes.

claim: A death in a diabetic patient could have been triggered by an undetected SARS-CoV-2 infection, resulting in a primary code of diabetes, with a SARS-CoV-2 code either lacking or listed as contributing condition.
source: For instance, a death in a diabetic patient could have been triggered by an undetected SARS-CoV-2 infection, resulting in a primary code of diabetes, with a SARS-CoV-2 code either lacking or listed as contributing condition.
evidence: The claim is based on inference about death certification practices and disease interactions.

claim: Mortality from chronic conditions rises concomitantly with influenza-associated respiratory mortality in epidemic and pandemic seasons.
source: A similar phenomenon has been reported for influenza, with mortality from chronic conditions rising concomitantly with influenza-associated respiratory mortality in epidemic and pandemic seasons (Reichert et al., 2004; Quandelacy et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research on influenza mortality patterns.

claim: There was substantial geographic and temporal heterogeneity in the trajectory of the COVID-19 pandemic in the United States.
source: In the United States, there was substantial geographic and temporal heterogeneity in the trajectory of the COVID-19 pandemic, along with differences in the strength and types of interventions implemented to mitigate COVID-19.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about the pandemic's progression in the United States.

claim: There were differences in the strength and types of interventions implemented to mitigate COVID-19 across the United States.
source: In the United States, there was substantial geographic and temporal heterogeneity in the trajectory of the COVID-19 pandemic, along with differences in the strength and types of interventions implemented to mitigate COVID-19.
evidence: The claim is based on established knowledge about pandemic response measures in the United States.

claim: From March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022, there were 848,866 cumulative deaths officially attributed to COVID-19 in the United States.
source: Across the United States from March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022, there were 848,866 cumulative deaths officially attributed to COVID-19, namely, with COVID-19 as the underlying cause of death.
evidence: The claim is based on official mortality data from the National Center for Health Statistics.

claim: From March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022, there were 757,600 (95% CI 725,200–788,100) excess respiratory deaths in the United States.
source: During the same period, we estimate 757,600 (95% Confidence Intervals (CI) 725,200–788,100) excess respiratory deaths and 1,065,200 (95% CI 909,800–1,218,000) excess deaths due to all-cause (Table 1).
evidence: The claim is based on excess mortality analysis of respiratory disease data.

claim: National mortality patterns comprise four waves from March 1, 2020 to November 11, 2021.
source: National mortality patterns comprise four waves from March 1 to June 20, 2020 (wild-type variant); June 21 to September 19, 2020 (wild-type variant); September 20, 2020 to June 19, 2021 (wild-type and Alpha variants); June 20 to November 11, 2021 (Delta variant).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of temporal patterns in mortality data.

claim: The first wave of COVID-19 mortality (March 1 to June 20, 2020) was caused by the wild-type variant.
source: National mortality patterns comprise four waves from March 1 to June 20, 2020 (wild-type variant); June 21 to September 19, 2020 (wild-type variant); September 20, 2020 to June 19, 2021 (wild-type and Alpha variants); June 20 to November 11, 2021 (Delta variant).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of SARS-CoV-2 variant circulation patterns.

claim: The fourth wave of COVID-19 mortality (June 20 to November 11, 2021) was caused by the Delta variant.
source: National mortality patterns comprise four waves from March 1 to June 20, 2020 (wild-type variant); June 21 to September 19, 2020 (wild-type variant); September 20, 2020 to June 19, 2021 (wild-type and Alpha variants); June 20 to November 11, 2021 (Delta variant).
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of SARS-CoV-2 variant circulation patterns.

claim: A recrudescence of mortality in the last weeks of 2021 was attributable to the co-circulation of the Delta and Omicron variants.
source: A recrudescence of mortality in the last weeks of 2021 was attributable to the co-circulation of the Delta and Omicron variants.
evidence: The claim is based on knowledge of variant circulation and temporal patterns in mortality data.

claim: The timing and intensity of mortality varied greatly by state.
source: The timing and intensity of mortality varied greatly by state (Figure 1A and Appendix 1—figures 1–8).
evidence: The claim is supported by state-specific mortality data shown in figures.

claim: The first wave of COVID-19 mortality was concentrated in Northeastern states.
source: The first wave was concentrated in Northeastern states, while Southern and Western states experienced mortality increases during later waves.
evidence: The claim is based on geographic analysis of mortality data.

claim: Southern and Western states experienced mortality increases during later waves of COVID-19.
source: The first wave was concentrated in Northeastern states, while Southern and Western states experienced mortality increases during later waves.
evidence: The claim is based on geographic analysis of mortality data.

claim: All-cause and respiratory disease excess mortality estimates, as well as national estimates, were robust to the choice of the calibration period.
source: All-cause and respiratory disease estimates, as well as national estimates, were particularly robust to the choice of the calibration period.
evidence: The claim is based on sensitivity analysis shown in Appendix 1—figure 9.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence ranged between 11.1 and 47.7% across states as of late December 2021.
source: Seroprevalence estimates ranged between 11.1 and 47.7% across states, with a population-weighted national seroprevalence of 34.6%.
evidence: The claim is based on CDC seroprevalence survey data.

claim: The population-weighted national SARS-CoV-2 seroprevalence was 34.6% as of late December 2021.
source: Seroprevalence estimates ranged between 11.1 and 47.7% across states, with a population-weighted national seroprevalence of 34.6%.
evidence: The claim is based on CDC seroprevalence survey data.

claim: New York and Alabama experienced higher than predicted excess mortality with respect to their reported serologic infection rates.
source: New York and Alabama experienced higher than predicted excess mortality with respect to their reported serologic infection rates, while Illinois and Michigan had the reverse pattern.
evidence: The claim is based on regression analysis of excess mortality against seroprevalence.

claim: Illinois and Michigan had lower than predicted excess mortality with respect to their reported serologic infection rates.
source: New York and Alabama experienced higher than predicted excess mortality with respect to their reported serologic infection rates, while Illinois and Michigan had the reverse pattern.
evidence: The claim is based on regression analysis of excess mortality against seroprevalence.

claim: The nationwide infection fatality rate (IFR) was estimated at 0.67% (95% CI 0.60–0.73%) based on excess respiratory mortality.
source: The nationwide infection fatality rate (IFR) was estimated at 0.67% (95% CI 0.60–0.73%) based on excess respiratory mortality and 0.89% (95% CI 0.77–1.02%) based on all-cause excess mortality (Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation using excess respiratory mortality and seroprevalence data.

claim: The nationwide infection fatality rate (IFR) was estimated at 0.89% (95% CI 0.77–1.02%) based on all-cause excess mortality.
source: The nationwide infection fatality rate (IFR) was estimated at 0.67% (95% CI 0.60–0.73%) based on excess respiratory mortality and 0.89% (95% CI 0.77–1.02%) based on all-cause excess mortality (Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation using all-cause excess mortality and seroprevalence data.

claim: The IFR based on official COVID-19 deaths was 0.72% (95%CI 0.62–0.81%).
source: Use of official COVID-19 deaths determined an IFR of 0.72% (95%CI 0.62–0.81%); interestingly, serology was more highly correlated with excess respiratory deaths than with official COVID-19 deaths (Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: The claim is based on calculation using official COVID-19 deaths and seroprevalence data.

claim: Serology was more highly correlated with excess respiratory deaths than with official COVID-19 deaths.
source: Use of official COVID-19 deaths determined an IFR of 0.72% (95%CI 0.62–0.81%); interestingly, serology was more highly correlated with excess respiratory deaths than with official COVID-19 deaths (Appendix 1—figure 10).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis comparing different mortality measures with seroprevalence.

claim: The IFR was significantly higher in individuals over 65 years, estimated at 5.5% (95% CI 4.5–6.6%) based on all-cause excess respiratory mortality.
source: The IFR was significantly higher in individuals over 65 years, estimated at 5.5% (95% CI 4.5–6.6%) based on all-cause excess respiratory mortality.
evidence: The claim is based on age-stratified analysis of excess mortality and seroprevalence.

claim: On a national level, over a 5 month period (November 2020 to March 2021), the mortality burden of COVID-19 was 5.7-fold higher than that of influenza (November 2017 to March 2018) based on all-cause excess mortality.
source: We find that nationally, over this 5 month period, the mortality burden of COVID-19 was 5.7-fold higher than that of influenza based on all-cause excess mortality.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of excess mortality during COVID-19 and influenza seasons.

claim: The median ratio of COVID-19 to influenza excess mortality rates across states was 5.8 (IQR, 5.0–7.8).
source: A similar pattern was seen in all states median ratio of COVID-19 to influenza excess mortality rates across states, 5.8 (IQR, 5.0–7.8), (Appendix 1—figure 11).
evidence: The claim is based on state-level comparison of excess mortality during COVID-19 and influenza seasons.

claim: During the March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022 pandemic period, excess mortality increased for 6 of the 7 non-respiratory conditions studied.
source: Overall, during the March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022 pandemic period, excess mortality increased for 6 of the 7 non-respiratory conditions studied, although the timing and intensity of the rise varied by disease (Table 2, Figure 2).
evidence: The claim is based on cause-specific excess mortality analysis.

claim: Cancer was the only mortality condition that did not increase during the pandemic.
source: Cancer was the only mortality condition that did not increase during the pandemic.
evidence: The claim is based on cause-specific excess mortality analysis.

claim: Cancer deaths have remained below historic levels since March 2020.
source: Cancer deaths have remained below historic levels since March 2020, although cumulative departures from baseline were not significantly different from zero (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of cancer mortality data during the pandemic.

claim: Cumulative departures from baseline for cancer mortality were not significantly different from zero during the pandemic.
source: Cancer deaths have remained below historic levels since March 2020, although cumulative departures from baseline were not significantly different from zero (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is based on statistical analysis of cancer excess mortality.

claim: Mortality from chronic conditions such as Alzheimer's, diabetes, and heart disease rose during the pandemic.
source: In contrast, mortality from chronic conditions such as Alzheimer's, diabetes, and heart disease rose during the pandemic, with the trajectory of excess mortality matching the pattern of respiratory mortality in the 4 pandemic waves (Figure 2 for national patterns, and Appendix 1—figures 3–8 for state-specific data).
evidence: The claim is based on cause-specific excess mortality analysis.

claim: The trajectory of excess mortality from Alzheimer's, diabetes, and heart disease matched the pattern of respiratory mortality in the 4 pandemic waves.
source: In contrast, mortality from chronic conditions such as Alzheimer's, diabetes, and heart disease rose during the pandemic, with the trajectory of excess mortality matching the pattern of respiratory mortality in the 4 pandemic waves (Figure 2 for national patterns, and Appendix 1—figures 3–8 for state-specific data).
evidence: The claim is based on temporal correlation analysis of cause-specific mortality patterns.

claim: Across chronic conditions, the first excess mortality peaks occurred within one week of the first respiratory mortality peak on April 18, 2020.
source: Across these causes of death, the first excess mortality peaks occurred within one week of the first respiratory mortality peak on April 18, 2020, with the most pronounced synchronicity patterns observed in the first wave in New York and New Jersey.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of cause-specific mortality peaks.

claim: The most pronounced synchronicity patterns between respiratory and chronic condition mortality were observed in the first wave in New York and New Jersey.
source: Across these causes of death, the first excess mortality peaks occurred within one week of the first respiratory mortality peak on April 18, 2020, with the most pronounced synchronicity patterns observed in the first wave in New York and New Jersey.
evidence: The claim is based on state-specific temporal correlation analysis.

claim: Across chronic conditions, the peak of excess mortality was highest during the winter of 2020 to 21, or the third wave of the pandemic.
source: Across chronic conditions, the peak of excess mortality was highest during the winter of 2020 to 21, or the third wave of the pandemic (Appendix 1—figure 12).
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of cause-specific mortality peaks.

claim: There was a significant rise in deaths from external causes during the pandemic period from March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022, corresponding to 102,800 (95% CI 81,400–123,700) cumulative excess deaths nationally.
source: We found a significant rise in deaths from external causes during the pandemic period from March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022, corresponding to 102,800 (95% CI 81,400–123,700) cumulative excess deaths nationally (Figure 2 and Table 2).
evidence: The claim is based on excess mortality analysis of external causes.

claim: The largest excess mortality rates from external causes were found in states that also had high baseline death rates from these conditions.
source: The largest excess mortality rates from external causes were found in states that also had high baseline death rates from these conditions (Appendix 1—figure 13).
evidence: The claim is based on state-level correlation analysis of baseline and excess mortality from external causes.

claim: The weekly trajectory of mortality from external causes did not align with that of respiratory mortality.
source: However, the weekly trajectory of mortality from external causes did not align with that of respiratory mortality.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal correlation analysis of external cause and respiratory mortality.

claim: The largest excess death tolls from external causes during March 2020 to January 2022 were from accidents and injuries (43,600 excess deaths, 95% CI 17,200–70,000, a 12% increase over baseline).
source: The largest excess death tolls observed during this period were from accidents and injuries (43,600 excess deaths (95% CI 17,200–70,000), a 12% increase over baseline), drug overdoses (25,300 deaths (95% CI 12,000–38,700), 16% increase), and assaults and homicides (8,000 deaths (95% CI 3,700–12,200), 20% increase, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is based on subcategory analysis of external cause mortality.

claim: There were 25,300 excess deaths (95% CI 12,000–38,700) from drug overdoses during March 2020 to January 2022, representing a 16% increase over baseline.
source: The largest excess death tolls observed during this period were from accidents and injuries (43,600 excess deaths (95% CI 17,200–70,000), a 12% increase over baseline), drug overdoses (25,300 deaths (95% CI 12,000–38,700), 16% increase), and assaults and homicides (8,000 deaths (95% CI 3,700–12,200), 20% increase, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is based on subcategory analysis of external cause mortality.

claim: There were 8,000 excess deaths (95% CI 3,700–12,200) from assaults and homicides during March 2020 to January 2022, representing a 20% increase over baseline.
source: The largest excess death tolls observed during this period were from accidents and injuries (43,600 excess deaths (95% CI 17,200–70,000), a 12% increase over baseline), drug overdoses (25,300 deaths (95% CI 12,000–38,700), 16% increase), and assaults and homicides (8,000 deaths (95% CI 3,700–12,200), 20% increase, Table 3).
evidence: The claim is based on subcategory analysis of external cause mortality.

claim: Overdoses were the first subcategory of external causes to peak in May 2020.
source: Overdoses were the first to peak in May 2020, followed by accidents and assaults in July 2020.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of subcategories of external cause mortality.

claim: Accidents and assaults peaked in July 2020.
source: Overdoses were the first to peak in May 2020, followed by accidents and assaults in July 2020.
evidence: The claim is based on temporal analysis of subcategories of external cause mortality.

claim: Mortality from suicides remained at historic levels throughout the end of the study period.
source: Notably, mortality from suicides remained at historic levels throughout the end of the study period.
evidence: The claim is based on analysis of suicide mortality data during the pandemic.

claim: During the period March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022, all-cause mortality became more correlated with excess deaths from respiratory conditions in all 16 states with available respiratory estimates compared to historical patterns.
source: During the period March 1, 2020 to January 1, 2022, and compared to historical patterns, all-cause mortality became more correlated with excess deaths from respiratory conditions in all 16 states with available respiratory estimates (Appendix 1—figure 14 and methods for details).
evidence: The claim is based on correlation analysis comparing pandemic and pre-pandemic periods.

claim: States that experienced high cumulative excess respiratory deaths had concomitantly high excess mortality from all-causes (Spearman rho=0.81, 95% CI: 0.48–0.94).
source: States that experienced high cumulative excess respiratory deaths had concomitantly high excess mortality from all-causes (Spearman rho=0.81, 95% CI: 0.48–0.94), attesting to the large impact of COVID-19 on total mortality (Appendix 1—figure 15).
evidence: The claim is based on state-level correlation analysis of respiratory and all-cause excess mortality.

claim: Synchrony between excess deaths from underlying respiratory diseases and excess deaths from underlying chronic conditions increased during the pandemic in a subset of states.
source: Synchrony between excess deaths from underlying respiratory diseases and excess deaths from underlying chronic conditions increased during the pandemic in a subset of states (Appendix 1—figure 14), particularly for diabetes (n=8 states), Alzheimer's (n=5), heart diseases (n=4), and cerebrovascular diseases (n=4).
evidence: The claim is based on state-level synchronicity analysis of cause-specific mortality.

claim: Synchrony between respiratory and diabetes mortality increased during the pandemic in 8 states.
source: Synchrony between excess deaths from underlying respiratory diseases and excess deaths from underlying chronic conditions increased during the pandemic in a subset of states (Appendix 1—figure 14), particularly for diabetes (n=8 states), Alzheimer's (n=5), heart diseases (n=4), and cerebrovascular diseases (n=4).
evidence: The claim is based on state-level synchronicity analysis.

claim: Excess deaths recorded as due to cancer or external causes showed either no change or declining synchrony with respiratory mortality during the pandemic in most states.
source: In contrast, excess deaths recorded as due to cancer or external causes showed either no change (in most states) or declining synchrony (in one or two states) with respiratory mortality during the pandemic.
evidence: The claim is based on state-level synchronicity analysis of cause-specific mortality.

claim: There was a major direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection on mortality from all-cause, diabetes, heart disease, cerebrovascular diseases, and Alzheimer's based on GAM analysis.
source: We found a major direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection on mortality from all-cause, diabetes, heart disease, cerebrovascular diseases, and Alzheimer's; namely, the strongest predictor of excess mortality from these causes was COVID-19 deaths.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis using COVID-19 deaths as a predictor.

claim: The strongest predictor of excess mortality from all-cause, diabetes, heart disease, cerebrovascular diseases, and Alzheimer's was COVID-19 deaths.
source: We found a major direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection on mortality from all-cause, diabetes, heart disease, cerebrovascular diseases, and Alzheimer's; namely, the strongest predictor of excess mortality from these causes was COVID-19 deaths.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis comparing predictor variables.

claim: The relationship between chronic condition mortality and COVID-19 deaths, while non-linear, was typically monotonically increasing.
source: The relationship between these mortality conditions and COVID-19 deaths, while non-linear, was typically monotonically increasing.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis showing functional relationships.

claim: Non-pharmaceutical interventions and ICU occupancy variables were statistically associated with excess mortality.
source: Non-pharmaceutical interventions and ICU occupancy variables were also statistically associated with excess mortality, although the form of the relationship was more complex.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis.

claim: Non-pharmaceutical intervention variables had a curvilinear relationship with excess deaths.
source: Non-pharmaceutical intervention variables had a curvilinear relationship with excess deaths, consistent with different mechanisms affecting different periods of the pandemic.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis showing functional relationships.

claim: At lower levels of interventions (Oxford contingency index between 0 and 50), representing the early stages of the lockdown in March 2020, excess mortality rose with interventions.
source: At lower levels of interventions (measured by the Oxford contingency index between 0 and 50), representing the early stages of the lockdown in March 2020, excess mortality rose with interventions.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis of the relationship between intervention stringency and mortality.

claim: Later in the pandemic, increased interventions were estimated to have a beneficial effect on excess mortality.
source: Later in the pandemic, increased interventions were estimated to have a beneficial effect on excess mortality, driven by comparison between late 2020 when interventions were strengthened in response to increasing COVID-19 activity (Oxford index above 60), and Spring 2021 when interventions were relaxed (Oxford index between 50 and 60).
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis of the relationship between intervention stringency and mortality at different time periods.

claim: The best model fit among cause-specific mortality models was for all-cause mortality (R2=96%).
source: Furthermore, all mortality conditions were not equally well captured by our models: the best model fit was for all-cause mortality (R2=96%) and the worst was for cerebrovascular diseases (R2=47%; Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on model fit statistics from GAM analysis.

claim: The worst model fit among cause-specific mortality models was for cerebrovascular diseases (R2=47%).
source: Furthermore, all mortality conditions were not equally well captured by our models: the best model fit was for all-cause mortality (R2=96%) and the worst was for cerebrovascular diseases (R2=47%; Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is based on model fit statistics from GAM analysis.

claim: 70% (95% CI 45–89%) of Alzheimer's excess deaths were attributable to the direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: On a national level, the GAM approach estimated that 84% (95% CI 65–94%) of all-cause excess deaths were attributable to the direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection, while the proportion was 73% (95% CI, 32–94%) for heart diseases, 70% (95% CI: 45–89%) for Alzheimer's, and 70% (95% CI: 45–93%) for diabetes (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis estimating attributable fractions.

claim: 70% (95% CI 45–93%) of diabetes excess deaths were attributable to the direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: On a national level, the GAM approach estimated that 84% (95% CI 65–94%) of all-cause excess deaths were attributable to the direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection, while the proportion was 73% (95% CI, 32–94%) for heart diseases, 70% (95% CI: 45–89%) for Alzheimer's, and 70% (95% CI: 45–93%) for diabetes (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis estimating attributable fractions.

claim: 73% (95% CI 32–94%) of heart disease excess deaths were attributable to the direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: On a national level, the GAM approach estimated that 84% (95% CI 65–94%) of all-cause excess deaths were attributable to the direct impact of SARS-CoV-2 infection, while the proportion was 73% (95% CI, 32–94%) for heart diseases, 70% (95% CI: 45–89%) for Alzheimer's, and 70% (95% CI: 45–93%) for diabetes (Table 2).
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis estimating attributable fractions.

claim: The contribution of COVID-19 on cerebrovascular disease mortality was not statistically significant.
source: The contribution of COVID-19 on cerebrovascular diseases was not statistically significant.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis.

claim: Cancer and external cause mortality were more strongly associated with the intervention and ICU occupancy variables than with COVID-19.
source: Applying a similar GAM approach to excess mortality from cancer and external causes revealed that these conditions were more strongly associated with the intervention and ICU occupancy variables than with COVID-19.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis comparing predictor variables.

claim: Stricter interventions were associated with a nearly linear increase in external cause mortality.
source: Stricter interventions were associated with a nearly linear increase in external cause mortality and a decline in cancer mortality.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis showing functional relationships.

claim: Stricter interventions were associated with a decline in cancer mortality.
source: Stricter interventions were associated with a nearly linear increase in external cause mortality and a decline in cancer mortality.
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis showing functional relationships.

claim: COVID-19 deaths had a negative effect on excess mortality from external causes.
source: COVID-19 deaths had a negative effect on excess mortality from external causes (i.e. high COVID-19 activity coincided with fewer excess deaths from external causes, Table 2).
evidence: The claim is based on GAM regression analysis.

claim: The model for cancer had the worst fit of all conditions studied (R2=18%).
source: The model for cancer had the worst fit of all conditions studied, while the model for external causes had an intermediate fit (R2=18% vs 58% respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on model fit statistics from GAM analysis.

claim: The model for external causes had an intermediate fit (R2=58%).
source: The model for cancer had the worst fit of all conditions studied, while the model for external causes had an intermediate fit (R2=18% vs 58% respectively).
evidence: The claim is based on model fit statistics from GAM analysis.

claim: The median proportion of all-cause excess deaths attributed to direct COVID-19 effects at the state level was 81% (inter-quartile range across states, 63–90%).
source: The median proportion of all-cause excess deaths attributed to direct COVID-19 effects was 81% by the GAM approach (inter-quartile range across states, 63–90%, Appendix 1—figure 17).
evidence: The claim is based on state-level GAM regression analysis.

claim: State-level analyses confirmed the direct impact of COVID-19 on Alzheimer's, diabetes, and heart diseases, although the effect size was generally attenuated compared to national analyses.
source: State-level analyses confirmed the direct impact of COVID-19 on Alzheimer's, diabetes, and heart diseases, although the effect size was generally attenuated compared to national analyses.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of state-level and national GAM regression analyses.

claim: Consistent with national analyses, the effect of COVID-19 on mortality from cerebrovascular disease and cancer was low or non-significant at the state level.
